danish.title: Ottende bog (1811–12) — Kapitel 20
paragraphs: Pierre blev ikke til middag, men forlod rummet og tog straks af sted. Han kørte gennem byen og ledte efter Anatole Kuragin, ved tanken om hvem blodet nu steg ham til hovedet, og han mærkede, det var svært at trække vejret. Han var ikke ved isbakkerne, heller ikke hos sigøjnerne eller hos Komoneno. Pierre kørte til Klubben. I Klubben gik alt sin vante gang. Medlemmerne, der samledes til middag, sad rundt om i grupper; de hilste på Pierre og talte om byens nyheder. Lakajen, der hilste på ham og kendte hans vaner og bekendtskaber, fortalte ham, at der var en plads til ham i den lille spisestue, og at fyrst Mikhail Zakharytj var i biblioteket, men at Pavel Timofejevitj endnu ikke var kommet. En af Pierres bekendte spurgte, mens de talte om vejret, om han havde hørt om Kuragins bortførelse af Rostova, som hele byen talte om, og om det var sandt. Pierre lo og sagde, det var vrøvl, for han var lige kommet fra familien Rostov. Han spurgte alle om Anatole. Én fortalte ham, at han endnu ikke var kommet, en anden, at han kom til middag. Pierre syntes det var underligt at se denne rolige, ligegyldige menneskemængde, der intet anede om, hvad der foregik i hans sjæl. Han gik frem og tilbage i balsalen, ventede til alle var kommet, og da Anatole ikke dukkede op, blev han ikke til middag, men kørte hjem.

Anatole, som Pierre ledte efter, spiste den dag til middag med Dolokhov og rådførte sig med ham om, hvordan denne uheldige affære kunne reddes. Det forekom ham nødvendigt at se Natasja. Om aftenen kørte han til sin søster for at drøfte, hvordan et møde kunne arrangeres. Da Pierre kom hjem efter forgæves at have ledt i hele Moskva, meddelte hans kammertjener ham, at fyrst Anatole var hos grevinden. Grevindens salon var fuld af gæster.

Pierre gik uden at hilse på sin kone, som han ikke havde set siden sin hjemkomst — i dette øjeblik var hun ham mere modbydelig end nogensinde — ind i salonen, og da han så Anatole, gik han hen til ham.
»Åh, Pierre,« sagde grevinden og gik hen til sin mand. »Du aner ikke, hvor ilde det er gået for vores Anatole...«

Hun standsede, da hun i sit hoveds fremskudte holdning, hans glødende øjne og hans beslutsomme gang genkendte de forfærdelige tegn på det raseri og den styrke, hun kendte og selv havde oplevet efter hans duel med Dolokhov.
»Hvor du er, er der last og ondskab!« sagde Pierre til sin kone. »Anatole, kom med mig! Jeg må tale med dig,« tilføjede han på fransk.
Anatole så sig om mod sin søster og rejste sig føjeligt, rede til at følge Pierre. Pierre greb hans arm, trak ham til sig og var ved at føre ham ud af rummet.
»Hvis du tillader dig i min salon...« hviskede Hélène, men Pierre svarede ikke og gik ud af rummet.
Anatole fulgte ham med sit sædvanlige flotte skridt, men hans ansigt røbede uro.
Da han var kommet ind i sit arbejdsværelse, lukkede Pierre døren og henvendte sig til Anatole uden at se på ham.
»Du lovede grevinde Rostova at gifte dig med hende og var i færd med at bortføre hende, er det ikke sandt?«
»Mon cher,« svarede Anatole (hele deres samtale foregik på fransk), »jeg anser mig ikke for forpligtet til at svare på spørgsmål stillet i den tone.«
Pierres allerede blege ansigt forvrededes af raseri. Han greb Anatole i uniformskraven med sin store hånd og ruskede ham fra side til side, til Anatoles ansigt udviste tilstrækkelig rædsel.
»Når jeg siger, at jeg må tale med dig!...« gentog Pierre.
»Jamen, hør nu, dette er dumt. Hvad?« sagde Anatole og pillede ved en knap i sin krave, der var revet løs med en stump af stoffet.
»Du er en slyngel og en skurk, og jeg ved ikke, hvad der afholder mig fra fornøjelsen af at smadre dit hoved med dette!« sagde Pierre, der udtrykte sig så kunstigt, fordi han talte fransk.
Han tog et tungt brevpresse og løftede det truende, men lagde det straks tilbage på plads.
»Lovede du at gifte dig med hende?«
»Jeg... jeg tænkte ikke over det. Jeg lovede det aldrig, fordi...«
Pierre afbrød ham.
»Har du nogen breve fra hende? Nogen breve?« sagde han og gik hen mod Anatole.
Anatole kiggede på ham og stak straks hånden i lommen og trak sin tegnebog frem.
Pierre tog det brev, Anatole rakte ham, og skubbede et bord til side, der stod i vejen, og kastede sig ned på sofaen.

»Jeg vil ikke bruge vold, vær ikke bange!« sagde Pierre som svar på en forskrækket gestus fra Anatole. »For det første, brevene,« sagde han, som om han gentog en lektie for sig selv. »For det andet,« fortsatte han efter en kort pause, idet han rejste sig og igen gik frem og tilbage i rummet, »skal du i morgen forlade Moskva.«
»Men hvordan kan jeg...?«

»For det tredje,« fortsatte Pierre uden at lytte til ham, »må du aldrig nævne et ord om, hvad der er foregået mellem dig og grevinde Rostova. Jeg ved, jeg ikke kan forhindre dig i det, men hvis du har en gnist samvittighed...« Pierre gik flere gange tavst frem og tilbage i rummet.
Anatole sad ved bordet og rynkede bryn, mens han bed sig i læben.

»Kan du dog ikke forstå, at foruden din fornøjelse findes der noget, der hedder andre menneskers lykke og fred, og at du ødelægger et helt liv for din fornøjelses skyld! Mor dig med kvinder som min kone — med dem er du i din ret, for de ved, hvad du vil. De er rustede mod dig af den samme erfaring med udsvævelser; men at love en ung pige at gifte sig med hende... at bedrage, at bortføre... Forstår du ikke, at det er lige så lavt som at slå en gammel mand eller et barn?...«
Pierre holdt inde og så på Anatole, ikke længere med et vredt, men med et spørgende blik.

»Det ved jeg ikke noget om, hvad?« sagde Anatole, der blev mere selvsikker, efterhånden som Pierre beherskede sin vrede. »Det ved jeg ikke og vil ikke vide,« sagde han uden at se på Pierre og med en let skælven i underkæben, »men De har brugt ord til mig — 'lavt' og så videre — som jeg som ærens mand ikke kan tillade nogen at bruge.«
Pierre stirrede forbavset på ham, ude af stand til at forstå, hvad han ville.
»Selvom det var på tomandshånd,« fortsatte Anatole, »kan jeg dog alligevel ikke...«
»Er det oprejsning, du vil have?« sagde Pierre ironisk.
»De kunne i det mindste tage Deres ord tilbage. Hvad? Hvis De vil have, at jeg gør, som De ønsker, hvad?«
»Jeg tager dem tilbage, jeg tager dem tilbage!« sagde Pierre, »og jeg beder dig tilgive mig.« Pierre kastede uvilkårligt et blik på den løse knap. »Og hvis du har brug for penge til rejsen...«
Anatole smilede. Udtrykket i det lave og krybende smil, som Pierre kendte så godt fra sin kone, fyldte ham med afsky.
»Åh, den usle og hjerteløse yngel!« udbrød han og forlod rummet.
Næste dag rejste Anatole til Petersborg.

english.title: Book Eight (1811 - 12) — Chapter 20
paragraphs: Pierre didn't stay for dinner but left the room and went away at once. He drove through the town looking for Anatole Kuragin, at the thought of whom the blood rushed to his heart and he felt difficulty breathing. He was not at the ice hills, nor at the gypsies', nor at Komoneno's. Pierre drove to the Club. At the Club all was going on as usual. The members gathering for dinner were sitting in groups; they greeted Pierre and spoke of the town news. The footman, knowing his habits and acquaintances, told him there was a place left for him in the small dining room, and that Prince Michael Zakharych was in the library, but that Paul Timofeevich had not yet arrived. One of Pierre's acquaintances, while chatting about the weather, asked if he had heard about Kuragin's abduction of Rostova — which was the talk of the town — and was it true? Pierre laughed and said it was nonsense, as he had just come from the Rostovs'. He asked everyone about Anatole. One man told him he hadn't come yet, and another that he was expected for dinner. Pierre felt it strange to see this calm, indifferent crowd of people who were unaware of what was going on in his soul. He paced through the ballroom, waited till everyone had arrived, and as Anatole didn't show up, didn't stay for dinner but drove home.

Anatole, whom Pierre was looking for, dined that day with Dolokhov, consulting him about how to fix this unfortunate business. It seemed essential to him to see Natasha. In the evening he drove to his sister's to discuss with her how to arrange a meeting. When Pierre returned home after vainly hunting all over Moscow, his valet informed him that Prince Anatole was with the countess. The countess's drawing room was full of guests.
Pierre, without greeting his wife — whom he had not seen since his return, and at that moment found more repulsive than ever — entered the drawing room and seeing Anatole went up to him.
"Ah, Pierre," said the countess, going up to her husband. "You don't know what trouble our Anatole..."

She stopped, seeing in the forward thrust of her husband's head, in his glowing eyes and his determined stride, the terrible signs of that rage and power she knew and had herself experienced after his duel with Dolokhov.
"Where you are, there is vice and evil!" said Pierre to his wife. "Anatole, come with me! I must speak to you," he added in French.
Anatole glanced at his sister and rose obediently, ready to follow Pierre. Pierre, taking him by the arm, pulled him toward himself and led him from the room.
"If you make a scene in my drawing room..." Helene whispered, but Pierre didn't reply and went out.
Anatole followed him with his usual casual step, but his face showed anxiety.
Having entered his study, Pierre closed the door and addressed Anatole without looking at him.
"You promised Countess Rostova to marry her and were about to elope with her — is that so?"
"My dear fellow," answered Anatole (their whole conversation was in French), "I don't consider myself obliged to answer questions put to me in that tone."

Pierre's face, already pale, became distorted with fury. He seized Anatole by the collar of his uniform with his big hand and shook him from side to side until Anatole's face showed sufficient terror.
"When I tell you that I must talk to you!..." repeated Pierre.
"Come now, this is ridiculous. What?" said Anatole, fingering a button on his collar that had been torn loose with a bit of cloth.
"You're a scoundrel and a villain, and I don't know what stops me from the pleasure of smashing your skull with this!" said Pierre — expressing himself so stiffly because he was speaking French.
He took a heavy paperweight and lifted it threateningly, but at once put it back in its place.
"Did you promise to marry her?"
"I... I didn't think of it. I never promised, because..."
Pierre interrupted him.
"Have you any letters of hers? Any letters?" he said, moving toward Anatole.
Anatole glanced at him and immediately thrust his hand into his pocket and drew out his wallet.
Pierre took the letter Anatole handed him and, pushing aside a table that stood in his way, threw himself on the sofa.

"I won't be violent, don't be afraid!" said Pierre in answer to a frightened gesture of Anatole's. "First — the letters," said he, as if reciting a lesson to himself. "Second," he continued after a short pause, rising again and pacing the room, "tomorrow you must get out of Moscow."
"But how can I?..."

"Third," Pierre went on without listening, "you must never breathe a word of what has passed between you and Countess Rostova. I know I can't prevent your doing so, but if you have a spark of conscience..." Pierre paced the room several times in silence.
Anatole sat at a table, frowning and biting his lips.

"After all, you must understand that besides your pleasure there is such a thing as other people's happiness and peace, and that you are ruining a whole life for the sake of your own amusement! Amuse yourself with women like my wife — with them you're within your rights, for they know what you want of them. They are armed against you by the same experience of depravity. But to promise a young girl to marry her... to deceive, to kidnap... Don't you understand that it is as contemptible as beating an old man or a child?..."
Pierre paused and looked at Anatole no longer with anger but with a questioning look.

"I don't know about that, eh?" said Anatole, growing more confident as Pierre mastered his fury. "I don't know that and don't want to," he said, not looking at Pierre and with a slight tremor of his lower jaw, "but you've used such words to me — 'contemptible' and so on — which as a man of honor I can't allow anyone to use."
Pierre looked at him with amazement, unable to understand what he wanted.
"Though it was a private conversation," Anatole continued, "still I can't..."
"Are you looking for satisfaction?" said Pierre ironically.
"You could at least take back your words. What? If you want me to do as you wish, eh?"
"I take them back, I take them back!" said Pierre, "and I ask you to forgive me." Pierre involuntarily glanced at the torn button. "And if you need money for your journey..."
Anatole smiled. The expression of that base and cringing smile, which Pierre knew so well in his wife, revolted him.
"Oh, vile and heartless breed!" he exclaimed, and left the room.
The next day Anatole left for Petersburg.
